title: Sensitive Periods in Behavior: Song, Language and Sight

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: During the {{c1::sensory}} phase of song learning, a young songbird listens to and memorizes a tutor’s song.
cards.back: The song memory is formed before it guides practice.
cards.quote: In the sensory phase the bird listens and memorizes.
cards.section: Song: listen first, practice later

cards.front: What does a songbird do during the sensorimotor phase of song learning?
cards.back: It practices vocal sounds and gradually shapes them to match its memory of the tutor’s song.
cards.quote: In the sensorimotor phase it practices, producing rambling sounds that it gradually shapes until they match the memory.
cards.section: Song: listen first, practice later

cards.front: How does an auditory template guide a young songbird’s practice?
cards.back: The memorized tutor song supplies a target; hearing its own practice lets the bird compare its output with that target and correct it.
cards.quote: an auditory memory, laid down in the sensory phase, against which the bird compares and corrects its own practice.
cards.section: Song: listen first, practice later

cards.front: A young sparrow hears its tutor but loses hearing before vocal practice. Its adult song is abnormal. Which requirement for successful copying does this isolate?
cards.back: Auditory feedback during practice is required. Prior exposure supplied a tutor memory, but the bird could no longer hear and correct its own voice.
cards.quote: Hearing the tutor was not enough: the bird must hear itself to correct its voice.
cards.section: Song: listen first, practice later

cards.front: Why did Marler record adult white-crowned sparrow song after playing tutor recordings at different juvenile ages?
cards.back: Adult song measures the lasting effect of tutoring. Good copies after early tapes, but little effect of later tapes, reveal an age-dependent learning window.
cards.quote: The same tape, played at different ages, left very different marks.
cards.section: Song: listen first, practice later

cards.front: What is a developmental window for an experience?
cards.back: A range of ages when that experience has an unusually strong lasting effect compared with the same experience at other ages under comparable conditions.
cards.quote: A developmental window is a range of ages when an experience has an unusually strong lasting effect,
cards.section: How sharp is the window?

cards.front: Under the outcome-curve convention used here, how do critical and sensitive periods differ?
cards.back: A critical period shows an abrupt drop in lasting effect with later input; a sensitive period shows a gradual decline. The whole curve distinguishes them.
cards.quote: Telling them apart takes the shape of the whole curve, not a single summary number.
cards.section: How sharp is the window?

cards.front: Under comparable conditions, the same training leaves progressively smaller lasting gains across many starting ages, without a sudden drop. What kind of developmental window does this predict, and why?
cards.back: A sensitive period under the outcome-curve convention: the lasting effect declines gradually with later input rather than dropping abruptly.
cards.quote: Telling them apart takes the shape of the whole curve, not a single summary number.
cards.section: How sharp is the window?

cards.front: You suspect an unfamiliar learned behavior has an age window. How would you distinguish a critical from a sensitive period without confusing input differences with age effects?
cards.back: Give comparable input at multiple ages under comparable conditions, then measure a lasting outcome. Plot outcome against input age: an abrupt fall supports a critical period; a gradual fall supports a sensitive period under the stated convention.
cards.quote: Same input, different ages: measure what lasts.
cards.section: How sharp is the window?

cards.front: A young male zebra finch normally memorizes a tutor between about {{c1::25 and 65 days}} after hatching.
cards.back: The sensory and sensorimotor phases overlap; song crystallizes by about three months.
cards.quote: A young male memorizes a tutor, usually his father, between about 25 and 65 days after hatching,
cards.section: Who closes the window?

cards.front: Two male zebra finches first meet a new tutor at the same late age. One heard adult males early; the other did not. If hearing a tutor helps close the window, what difference is expected and why?
cards.back: The deprived bird may still copy the new tutor when the socially reared bird no longer does. Their equal ages make different experience histories relevant; reported results support this prediction, but later findings were mixed.
cards.quote: Same age, different history, different outcome.
cards.section: Who closes the window?

cards.front: Why does late copying by zebra finches reared without adult males not prove that tutor song alone controls window closure?
cards.back: The groups also differ in social and visual contact with adults, and later studies gave mixed results. Tutor exposure is not the only changing factor.
cards.quote: the groups differ in more than tutor exposure, such as social and visual contact with adults.
cards.section: Who closes the window?

cards.front: A male zebra finch is kept without a tutor well beyond the normal learning window. Should it remain indefinitely ready to copy a late tutor, and why?
cards.back: No. Deprivation can delay closure but does not abolish it: untutored birds eventually crystallize their own song. Even a successful late copy may be incomplete.
cards.quote: Missing input delays the closing but does not abolish it: birds kept without a tutor eventually crystallize a song of their own.
cards.section: Who closes the window?

cards.front: What is the motor pathway from HVC to the songbird’s vocal organ?
cards.back: HVC → RA → brainstem motor neurons controlling the syrinx.
cards.quote: The motor pathway: HVC to RA to the brainstem motor neurons of the syrinx.
cards.section: Which circuit matters while song is learned?

cards.front: The songbird anterior forebrain pathway runs HVC → area X → thalamus → {{c1::LMAN}} → RA.
cards.back: The loop leaves the motor pathway and rejoins it at RA.
cards.quote: The anterior forebrain pathway: HVC to area X, then the thalamus, then the nucleus LMAN, and from LMAN back to RA.
cards.section: Which circuit matters while song is learned?

cards.front: What does the different effect of juvenile and adult LMAN lesions in male zebra finches reveal?
cards.back: Juvenile lesions disrupt song development; adult lesions spare stable song. LMAN contributes to learning rather than being required to produce already learned song.
cards.quote: LMAN lesions in juveniles disrupted song development but did not affect stable song in adults.
cards.section: Which circuit matters while song is learned?

cards.front: Why can an NMDA receptor act as a detector of coincident neuronal activity?
cards.back: Glutamate signals sending-cell activity; receiving-cell depolarization removes the magnesium block. With a co-agonist bound, current can flow when both conditions coincide.
cards.quote: The glutamate comes from the cell sending the signal, and the depolarization reflects activity in the receiving cell.
cards.section: Which circuit matters while song is learned?

cards.front: A receiving neuron depolarizes enough to remove the NMDA receptor’s magnesium block, but no glutamate binds. Will NMDA receptor current flow, and why?
cards.back: No. Removing magnesium alone is insufficient: activation also requires glutamate and a co-agonist. The coincidence rule needs ligand binding as well as receiving-cell depolarization.
cards.quote: Glutamate and a co-agonist, glycine or D-serine (a second molecule that must bind alongside glutamate), activate the receptor.
cards.section: Which circuit matters while song is learned?

cards.front: AP5 near LMAN during zebra finch tutoring reduces later copying; the same drug there on non-tutoring days or in the cerebellum does not. What requirement does this pattern support?
cards.back: NMDA receptors in the anterior forebrain are needed during tutor memorization. The timing and regional controls tie the deficit to that learning step without identifying the memory’s storage site.
cards.why: Normal copying after AP5 on non-tutoring days weakens a practice-deficit explanation, but does not exclude it: birds could compensate on drug-free days.
cards.quote: The result places a requirement for NMDA receptors in that region, during tutoring, in the step of memorizing, without showing where the memory is stored.
cards.section: Which circuit matters while song is learned?

cards.front: Why does normal song discrimination in AP5-treated zebra finches matter when interpreting poor tutor copying?
cards.back: It argues against simple deafness to the songs as the explanation for poor copying; treated birds still distinguished zebra finch from canary song.
cards.quote: Treated birds could also still tell zebra finch song from canary song, so they were not simply deaf to it.
cards.section: Which circuit matters while song is learned?

cards.front: In male zebra finch experiments, juvenile LMAN lesions and anterior forebrain NMDA blockade during tutoring both impair song learning. Do these results locate the tutor memory in LMAN? Explain using the distinction between necessity and storage.
cards.back: No. Lesions show a pathway is needed during learning, and timed blockade shows a local receptor requirement during memorization. The rule is that disrupting a necessary step does not by itself identify where the resulting memory is stored.
cards.quote: The anterior forebrain pathway matters while song is learned, though the lesions alone cannot say where the tutor memory is kept.
cards.section: Which circuit matters while song is learned?

cards.front: What first-language claim did Lenneberg’s critical period hypothesis make?
cards.back: A first language can be acquired only between early childhood and puberty.
cards.quote: a first language can be acquired only between early childhood and puberty.
cards.section: Language: what the age effects do and do not show

cards.front: Why is severe childhood isolation a confounded test of whether missing early language causes lasting language difficulties?
cards.back: Isolation removes much more than language, including care and social contact. Later difficulties cannot be attributed specifically to the timing of language access.
cards.quote: But a child deprived so completely was deprived of much more than language, and such cases cannot isolate a language window.
cards.section: Language: what the age effects do and do not show

cards.front: In the ASL comparison of late first-language and late second-language learners, what did poorer performance by the first-language group suggest?
cards.back: Missing an accessible early language leaves lasting effects beyond learning sign late. Different ages of hearing loss limit the comparison as a causal test.
cards.quote: The first-language group did worse. The groups also differed in when they lost their hearing, so this is not a perfect control.
cards.section: Language: what the age effects do and do not show

cards.front: Two groups begin learning sign at the same age, but only one had an accessible earlier language. Why would matching the groups’ hearing-loss histories improve the comparison?
cards.back: It reduces a competing explanation for later proficiency differences. Matching learning age alone does not separate prior language access from differences in hearing-loss history; the groups still would not be randomly assigned.
cards.quote: The groups also differed in when they lost their hearing, so this is not a perfect control.
cards.section: Language: what the age effects do and do not show

cards.front: Why can an age effect in second-language learning not uniquely demonstrate declining brain plasticity?
cards.back: Learners already have a first language that may interfere, and input may differ. An age effect alone cannot distinguish those explanations from changing plasticity.
cards.quote: a decline with age could come from a brain that has become less plastic or from a first language that gets in the way.
cards.section: What a second language can and cannot show

cards.front: Two language datasets have the same overall correlation between starting age and adult score. One shows a sudden step; the other a steady slope. Can the correlation classify their windows, and why?
cards.back: No. A step and a slope can produce similar overall correlations. Under the outcome-curve convention, inspect the age-specific shape to distinguish abrupt from graded changes.
cards.quote: a single correlation across all arrivals could come out much the same for a sudden step as for a steady slope.
cards.section: What a second language can and cannot show

cards.front: How did adult English grammar scores vary with arrival age in Johnson and Newport’s study?
cards.back: Arrivals aged 3–7 scored like native speakers; scores then fell steadily up to about puberty. Later scores were lower, widely variable, and no longer tracked arrival age.
cards.quote: Scores then fell steadily with age of arrival up to about puberty.
cards.section: What a second language can and cannot show

cards.front: Hartshorne and colleagues’ model estimated that grammar-learning ability stays high until about {{c1::age 17}}, then declines.
cards.back: This is a model-based estimate of learning ability, rather than a directly observed outcome curve.
cards.quote: Their answer: grammar-learning ability stays high until about age 17, then declines.
cards.section: What a second language can and cannot show

cards.front: In an illustrative toy grammar model, learning is at full speed until age 17 and native-like grammar needs 7 full-speed years. A learner starts at 13. How many full-speed years remain, and what is the shortfall?
cards.back: Available: 17 − 13 = 4 full-speed years. Shortfall: 7 − 4 = 3 full-speed years. These are toy assumptions, not measured requirements; learning can continue more slowly afterward.
cards.quote: That number is not a measurement: it is picked so the toy matches the model's conclusion below,
cards.section: What a second language can and cannot show

cards.front: How can adult grammar outcomes decline with starting age before a model predicts any decline in learning ability?
cards.back: The rule is that learning takes years. A later starter can initially learn just as well but have fewer years before a later slowdown. Thus a lasting-outcome curve need not reveal when learning ability itself changes.
cards.quote: So the curve of what lasts can start to fall in late childhood even if the ability to learn falls only in late adolescence.
cards.section: What a second language can and cannot show

cards.front: Zebra finch rearing histories can shift late tutor copying, and later human language access predicts lower proficiency. Do these together establish that experience closes the human language window?
cards.back: No. The rule is to separate causal manipulations from naturally differing histories. Animal evidence does not remove confounds in human comparisons or establish that the same closure mechanism operates across species.
cards.quote: whether from a change in the brain's plasticity, competition from an entrenched first language, or differences in the kind and amount of input is still debated.
cards.section: What a second language can and cannot show

cards.front: Visual {{c1::acuity}} is the finest detail the eye can resolve.
cards.back: It improves over the first years of life, steeply in the first year.
cards.quote: Acuity, the finest detail the eye can resolve, and contrast sensitivity, the ability to detect faint differences in brightness,
cards.section: Sight: separate windows for separate abilities

cards.front: What does contrast sensitivity measure?
cards.back: The ability to detect faint differences in brightness.
cards.quote: contrast sensitivity, the ability to detect faint differences in brightness, both improve over the first years of life,
cards.section: Sight: separate windows for separate abilities

cards.front: How does forced-choice preferential looking estimate an infant’s visual acuity without asking for a verbal report?
cards.back: An observer unaware of stripe location judges the infant’s gaze toward stripes versus equal-brightness gray. The finest grating reliably preferred estimates acuity in cycles per degree.
cards.quote: The finest grating the infant reliably looks at gives its acuity in cycles per degree, one cycle being one dark and one light stripe.
cards.section: Sight: separate windows for separate abilities

cards.front: After dense congenital cataracts were treated, infants of different ages initially had newborn-like acuity, with some improving within an hour of visual input. Which explanation does this challenge?
cards.back: It challenges age alone as sufficient for acuity improvement. The rapid change after patterned input supports an input requirement; it does not identify the cortical mechanism.
cards.quote: some improvement appeared after as little as an hour of visual input: improvement needs patterned input, not age alone.
cards.section: Sight: separate windows for separate abilities

cards.front: A child’s acuity begins improving soon after patterned vision is restored. Does that predict complete recovery of every visual function, and why?
cards.back: No. Different visual abilities have different sensitive periods, and early deprivation can leave lasting deficits. Initial improvement in acuity cannot establish full recovery of fine acuity or facial-spacing processing.
cards.quote: Different abilities were affected by deprivation at different ages, so different visual abilities have different sensitive periods.
cards.section: Sight: separate windows for separate abilities

cards.front: What makes a deprivation effect a sleeper effect in visual development?
cards.back: Deprivation occurs before an ability appears but impairs its later development. The later-emerging deficit shows that early input can matter before the function is behaviorally evident.
cards.quote: Some are affected by deprivation before the ability itself has appeared, which Maurer and colleagues call a sleeper effect.
cards.section: Sight: separate windows for separate abilities

cards.front: A study pools acuity and facial-spacing outcomes across several treatment ages to estimate one visual window. What analysis would better test whether the two functions share a window?
cards.back: Plot each function’s lasting outcome against treatment age separately under comparable exposure conditions. The rule is to keep curves separate for different functions and protocols; pooling can hide distinct sensitive periods.
cards.quote: Separate curves for different functions, species and exposure conditions.
cards.section: Putting it together

cards.front: In chick embryos, leg movements continue after sensory input to the lumbar spinal cord is removed. Does this result alone establish an experience-dependent developmental window, and why?
cards.back: No. In chick embryos, these movements are generated within the spinal cord. The window rule concerns lasting effects of specific experience on learned behavior; persistence without sensory input does not establish an input-age effect.
cards.quote: The earliest behaviors come from simple circuits that run on their own, without experience.
cards.section: Early movements that do not need experience

cards.front: Using Snellen denominator ≈ 20 × (30 ÷ acuity in cycles per degree), what approximate Snellen fraction corresponds to a finest grating of 3 cycles per degree?
cards.back: Denominator ≈ 20 × (30 ÷ 3) = 200, so acuity is approximately 20/200. This conversion is method-dependent.
cards.quote: Snellen denominator ≈ 20 × (30 ÷ finest grating in cycles per degree)
cards.section: Converting a grating to a Snellen fraction
